original_question: Among graphs that exhibit structural properties typical of power grids, what is the typical order of magnitude of the smallest (n-k)-contingent zero-forcing set as a function of the numbers of vertices and edges?
target_in_paper: Section 7, Open Problem 7.3: the problem of estimating the typical size of a minimum (n-k)-contingent zero-forcing set in graphs exhibiting structural properties characteristic of power grids.
correct_elements: The draft correctly targets the power-grid zero-forcing section, asks about minimum-size (n-k)-contingent zero-forcing sets rather than ordinary zero forcing, restricts attention to graphs meant to resemble power-grid networks rather than arbitrary graphs, and asks for dependence on graph size through the numbers of vertices and edges.
missing_details: The draft does not define ordinary zero forcing: starting from an initial blue set Z, one repeatedly applies the rule that a blue vertex with exactly one uncolored neighbor forces that neighbor blue, and Z is a zero-forcing set if this eventually colors all vertices.
The draft does not define an (n-k)-contingent zero-forcing set: for a graph G=(V,E), a set Z⊆V must remain a zero-forcing set of G'=(V,E\E') for every edge subset E' with |E'|≤k.
The contingency parameter k is implicit in the draft but should be stated explicitly as a fixed or given nonnegative integer (the paper uses k as the number of edge failures tolerated).
The optimization variable should be explicit: the question concerns the cardinality of a minimum subset Z⊆V satisfying the contingent zero-forcing condition.

The paper's phrase 'graphs exhibiting structural properties characteristic of power grids' is not formally axiomatized in Open Problem 7.3; nearby context motivates it by power-grid-like sparse, large-diameter, low-average-degree, long-cycle structure, but the problem itself leaves the class/model open.

The draft says 'typical order of magnitude,' whereas the paper asks for the 'typical size, in terms of the number of vertices and edges,' i.e. a rough size estimate rather than a sharper asymptotic theorem with a specified probabilistic model.
The nearby context also proves an equivalent formulation via k-leaky zero forcing (Lemma 7.7), which is useful if one wants an alternate stand-alone version.

There is no ambient ring, field, homogeneity, degree-of-polynomial, or nilpotency condition here; the ambient objects that need specification are only the graph G=(V,E), the vertex subset Z, and the contingency level k.
refined_question: For a given integer k≥1 and a graph G=(V,E), call Z⊆V an (n-k)-contingent zero-forcing set if, for every edge set E'⊆E with |E'|≤k, the set Z is a zero-forcing set of G'=(V,E\E'), where 'zero forcing' means that, starting with Z colored blue, one may repeatedly color any vertex that is the unique uncolored neighbor of a blue vertex until no more such moves are possible. When G ranges over graphs exhibiting structural properties characteristic of power grids, what is the typical size, as a function of |V| and |E|, of a minimum (n-k)-contingent zero-forcing set?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, by Lemma 7.7: for a given integer k≥1 and a graph G=(V,E), what is the typical size, as a function of |V| and |E|, of a minimum k-leaky zero-forcing set in graphs exhibiting structural properties characteristic of power grids, where Z⊆V is k-leaky if for every L⊆V with |L|≤k, Z is a zero-forcing set of the graph obtained from G by attaching a pendant vertex to each vertex of L?
justification: The draft is aimed at Open Problem 7.3, not the neighboring Open Problems 7.1 or 7.2. The paper's Section 7 first motivates contingent zero forcing by power-grid observability/control under changing topology, then defines ordinary zero forcing (Definitions 7.1-7.2) and (n-k)-contingent zero forcing (Definition 7.3). It next shows that trees are completely understood in this setting (Lemma 7.5), which is relevant because the paper describes typical power-grid graphs as structurally tree-like. Finally, after distinguishing the structural-characterization question (Open Problem 7.1) and the algorithmic question (Open Problem 7.2), it asks the size-estimation question in Open Problem 7.3. Your draft matches that third problem almost verbatim, but it needs the formal contingent-zero-forcing definition and the role of k to be fully stand-alone and paper-faithful.
